title: How much of the cost of a zero-emission German power system is the storage assumption, once costs are sourced?
summary: Re-runs energy-mix (one-node PyPSA model of Germany's 2019 hourly load with solar, onshore wind, gas, Li-ion and hydrogen storage under an emissions cap) with every cost, lifetime, O&M, efficiency, fuel price and CO2 intensity read from PyPSA technology-data at pinned revisions (Danish Energy Agency and other primary sources named per row). On 2030 costs in 2025 euros the unconstrained optimum costs EUR 75/MWh and zero emissions EUR 222/MWh with a steel hydrogen tank (1.3 TWh of hydrogen, 1.4 TWh of batteries) or EUR 144/MWh with underground storage (24.9 TWh); the last 5% of emissions costs about EUR 6,100/t with the tank and EUR 1,700/t with caverns. With caverns, technology-data's older 2030 and 2050 sets give EUR 114.5 and 85.5/MWh. Without batteries zero emissions costs EUR 254 (tank) or 162 (cavern); a discount rate of 3% or 10% gives EUR 152 or 282 (tank). Not from a source: the 7% discount rate (swept). Limitations: cavern storage is a geological resource that the model does not site or limit, one weather year, one node, no imports, central cost values only, and no check against a published whole-system figure.
lede: what does a zero-emission German power system cost once `energy-mix`'s assumed costs are replaced by sourced ones? PyPSA on 2019 hourly demand with PyPSA technology-data costs (Danish Energy Agency et al.): EUR 222/MWh with a steel hydrogen tank, EUR 144 with caverns, EUR 75 unconstrained; the storage type moves the answer more than the cost year.
